drivingQuestion: Does the mishna's mention of Jews alone exclude gentiles from the law of valuations?
outcomeNote: The inference is set up here; its testing against Rabbi Meir follows in the next unit.

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ יֵשׁ בַּעֲרָכִין לְהָקֵל וְכוּ׳ וּלְהַחְמִיר כֵּיצַד אֶחָד שֶׁהֶעֱרִיךְ כּוּ׳. בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל — אִין, בַּגּוֹיִם — לָא.
segments.en: «GEMARA:» The mishna states: «There are» halakhot «with regard to valuations that are lenient and» others «that are stringent; how so? Both» in the case of one «who took» a vow of «valuation» to donate the fixed value of the most attractive among the Jewish people «and» in the case of one who took a vow of valuation to donate the fixed value of the most unsightly among the Jewish people, he gives the fixed payment of fifty sela to the Temple treasury. The Gemara infers from this that if the vow of valuation referred «to a Jew, yes,» he pays the fixed value; but if one took a vow of valuation to donate the fixed value «of gentiles,» he does «not» pay the fixed value.

moves.summary: quotes the mishna's clause about valuating a Jew

moves.summary: infers that gentiles are excluded from the fixed valuation
moves.about: the mishna's restriction of the example to Jews implies that a vow of valuation upon a gentile does not take effect
